November 2009 # Legally striking CRU anticipated that in Q4 2009 there was going to be turmoil regarding negotiations of collective labour agreements at several major copper mine operations. A few weeks ago, the attention was focused on the start-up of negotiations at BHP Billiton’s Spence mine as it was expected to set a precedent for further bargaining at major operations including Escondida (BHP Billiton, Rio Tinto, JECO and IFC) and Chuquicamata (Codelco). These two are of especial interest as the negotiations will overlap with the forthcoming presidential elections. Early proposals from the managers of BHP Billiton and Codelco, however, and an uneasy environment at Spence have shaken up the market, whilst these actions have been raising supply-side concerns in the copper market. Likewise, the copper price reached the highest level in 13 months, and this encourages the claims of the mine workers. In this report, we aim to go briefly through the main issues of the Chilean recent collective labour agreements, their respective negotiations and the legal timeline of the negotiations process. Our main findings are: - The early offer accepted by the unionised workers at Escondida (operated by BHP Billiton) set a precedent as it has been the most generous deal for a collective labour agreement ever seen in Chile. - Copper mines in Chile that have pending negotiations for collective labour agreements account for 20% of the Chilean copper mine production. - The Chilean labour legislation sets a legal framework for unionised workers to negotiate their collective labour agreements. The legislation is not exclusive to the mining industry. In the second section of the report we describe, in a simplified version, the timeline of the negotiations for a collective labour agreement in Chile. The overall process – from the start of the official negotiations to the end of a likely longest strike period – can take as long as 85 days. © 2009 CRU International Limited **confidential** **November 2009** **www.crumonitor.com** ## **Family (and neighbours) ties** In Q3 2006, unionised workers at Escondida held a 25-day strike before agreeing a collective labour contract with the company. This strike was the longest and most harmful – in terms of production losses – for the industry in the recent Chilean history. In 2009, a similar scenario was expected as negotiations were due to start in early December, just a week before the presidential elections in Chile. However, an early offer to renew the collective labour agreement made by the managers was approved by 72% of the unionised workers. As a reference, the US$25,500 bonus is roughly between two and three times Chile’s GDP per capita, and would be considerably higher than an annual wage of an average worker in any other industry in Chile. In October 2009, aggressive negotiations reached a staltement at BHP Billiton’s Spence mine. The mine started-up in 2006 and the first collective labour agreement expired in September 2009. Unionised workers at Spence rejected offers made by the company’s management and have been on strike since October 13th , although there was an attempt to resume negotiations. The workers demands, according to press reports, consist of: 5.5% increase in wages, 24-month duration and US$27,250 bonuses (~US$13,750 per year). This is more ambitious than the deal recently reached at Escondida, and higher than the latest agreements of other copper mines in Chile (see table). CRU considers that BHP Billiton will be able to withstand the strike at Spence for a considerable period. The 25-day strike at Escondida set a benchmark, although it is not fully owned by BHP Billiton. Escondida produces six times more copper than Spence. The copper cash price in August 2006 (US$7,696/t) was 24% higher than the one in October 2009 (US$6,267/t as of 28th October). The market value of the production that was lost in 2006 was broadly US$317

M (US$182M attributable to BHP Billiton), and 16-day strike at Spence can be around US$48M (as of 29th October). Codelco Norte and Andina (two of the five mine operations of Codelco) will negotiate the renewal of their collective labour agreements in December 2009. For many people, the Escondida agreement sets a © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 6 **November 2009** www.crumonitor.com precedent to the negotiations at Codelco given the similarities between them in size and production levels. However, Codelco is a state-owned company, has a lower productivity and higher costs. Therefore, in this case, the presidential elections are more relevant than for other mines. The mines that are due to negotiate collective labour agreements in the next few months are expected to produce, altogether, 20% of the Chilean or 6% of the world’s copper mine production in 2009. A list of 2009 negotiations at South American mines is available in the June 2009 edition of the CRU Copper South America Monthly. ## **Timeline for the negotiations** In Chile, the collective labour agreements are ruled by the labour, not the mining, authorities. Therefore, the same legal framework applies across every industry. However, it has the greatest impact at copper mines, as workers are aware that mining companies are earning higher profits at the current copper price. The negotiation process can take as long as 85 days (including a strike) and during this time is unlikely that employees would work at their usual pace and productivity (see table).
